coherence_analysis.what_breaks_if_only_the_se_changes:
Take the system to be 'p-value from the pooled SE, interval switched to the unpooled Wald SE', with the decision still read off the interval. Five things break, in order of how much they matter.

(1) The exact equivalence dies, and it dies asymmetrically. 'CI excludes 0' is |dhat| > z*SE_u; 'p < alpha' is |dhat| > z*SE_0. They disagree exactly on the band where |dhat|/z lies between the two SEs. Let R = SE_0/SE_u. From the exact identity in the derivation (section 3), with n1=n2 = n per arm, SE_0^2 - SE_u^2 = dhat^2/N (N = n1+n2), so at the decision boundary dhat ~ z*SE_u we get R^2 = 1 + z^2/N, R - 1 ~ z^2/(2N). At z = 2.878 (alpha = 0.004) and N = 2e4 that is 2.1e-4: the two verdicts essentially never differ. Under H0 the disagreement probability is ~ 2*phi(z)*z*|R-1| = phi(z)*z^3/N = 0.151/N = 7.6e-6, which is 0.19% of the alpha budget. In a BALANCED design the whole controversy is a non-event.

(2) Under arm-size imbalance the same quantity becomes first-order. The exact identity has a term LINEAR in dhat that vanishes only at w = n1/N = 1/2: SE_0^2 - SE_u^2 = [ (1-2w)(1-2p1)*d + (w-(1-w)^2)*d^2 ] / (N*w*(1-w)). Near the boundary (valid while |d| << p) this gives R ~ 1 - gamma_D*z/2, where gamma_D = (1-2p)(2w-1)/( sqrt(N p q) * sqrt(w(1-w)) ) is exactly the standardized skewness of dhat under H0. Worked case, not exotic: an 80/20 holdout, p = 0.01, N = 1e5 (so the small arm still has 200 conversions -- nothing sparse about it). gamma_D = 0.98*0.6/(31.46*0.4) = 0.0467, so |R-1| = 6.7%. Disagreement probability = 2*phi(2.878)*2.878*0.067 = 2.4e-3 -- that is 61% as many events as there are rejections at alpha = 0.004. So: p < alpha shown next to a CI containing zero would be a routine, not rare, sight on imbalanced experiments.

(3) The decision rule itself changes, so every previously recorded A/A calibration certifies a rule that is no longer in force. This is the practical landmine: the FPR difference between the two rules is second-order (the two tails shift in opposite directions and largely cancel -- see derivation section 6), so the A/A matrix will report 'still calibrated' while the persisted verdicts on live imbalanced experiments have moved. A calibration that cannot see the change it is being asked to certify is worse than no calibration.

(4) Any downstream surface that re-derives significance from the persisted p-value rather than from the persisted interval will disagree with the one that reads the interval. Under the pooled-both design those two can never disagree; after the switch they can, at the rates in (1) and (2).

(5) Nothing else improves as much as it looks. The unpooled Wald interval is a better confidence set than the pooled one for a nonzero effect -- that is real and is the whole point -- but it is still first-order only, it still collapses to zero width at x = 0 or x = n, and it is still the interval whose coverage BCD (2001) indict. Switching only the SE buys validity-at-the-alternative and pays for it with incoherence, when a single extra step (invert the score family at every candidate value of the difference, not just at zero) buys both.
coherence_analysis.can_ci_and_pvalue_disagree: Under the pooled-SE-for-both design: never, by construction and exactly. Under pooled-p + unpooled-Wald-CI: yes, at a rate I can quantify in closed form. Balanced arms: P(disagree | H0) ~ phi(z)*z^3/N, e.g. 7.6e-6 per comparison at z=2.878, N=2e4 -- unobservable. Imbalanced arms: P(disagree | H0) ~ 2*phi(z)*z*|1-R| with 1-R ~ gamma_D*z/2, e.g. 2.4e-3 at an 80/20 split, p=0.01, N=1e5 -- comparable to alpha itself. The disagreement is SYSTEMATIC, not random: its sign is fixed by which arm is larger and which arm's phat is higher. When the smaller arm has the higher rate the pooled SE is the SMALLER of the two, so the p-value rejects while the interval covers zero; when the smaller arm has the lower rate the reverse. The width of the disagreement band grows linearly in z, so it widens as the multiplicity correction tightens alpha. Under an alternative the two SEs diverge much further (the d^2 term), but both then say 'significant' and only the reported WIDTH is wrong -- decision flips live at the boundary, which is precisely where the linear imbalance term dominates. Miettinen-Nurminen removes the possibility entirely: Z(0) is identically the pooled statistic, so 'the interval excludes zero' and 'p < alpha' are the same event by construction, with the interval still valid at every nonzero value. The one caveat is the MN N/(N-1) variance factor: applied to the interval only, it reintroduces a disagreement of relative size 1/(2N) (5e-5 at N=1e4) -- vanishing, but it should be applied to both or to neither so the equality is exact in floating point up to rounding.
coherence_analysis.recommendation: Define ONE statistic and use it three ways. The two-sample score statistic with constrained maximum-likelihood variance, Z(delta) = (phat2 - phat1 - delta)/sigma_tilde(delta), where sigma_tilde(delta)^2 = ptilde1*(1-ptilde1)/n1 + ptilde2*(1-ptilde2)/n2 and (ptilde1, ptilde2) maximize the binomial likelihood subject to ptilde2 - ptilde1 = delta. Then: the p-value is 2*(1 - Phi(|Z(0)|)) -- which is IDENTICALLY the pooled two-sample z (Pearson chi-square), so nothing about the reported p-value changes; the absolute interval is {delta : Z(delta)^2 <= z^2}; and the relative interval is the same construction on the ratio scale (section 15 of the derivation), whose statistic at ratio = 1 is again the very same pooled Z. All three are then coherent by construction, and the interval is a genuine confidence set everywhere, not only at zero. Apply the MN N/(N-1) factor to all three or to none. Ranking of the alternatives on the two axes that matter here: MN = coherent AND valid; Newcombe or a correctly alpha-scaled Agresti-Caffo interval beside a pooled p = valid but incoherent (with the disagreement rates above); unpooled Wald beside a pooled p = the textbook state, valid to first order, incoherent, and broken at boundaries; pooled SE for both = coherent and INVALID as an interval -- it is the worst option on the one thing an interval exists to do, and its defect is invisible to an A/A false-positive measurement.

derivation:
NOTATION. X_j ~ Bin(n_j, p_j) independent, j = 1 (control), 2 (treatment); phat_j = X_j/n_j; v(p) = p(1-p); q = 1-p; delta = p2 - p1; N = n1 + n2; w = n1/N; z = z_{1-alpha/2}; phi, Phi the standard normal density and cdf. Var(phat2 - phat1) = v(p1)/n1 + v(p2)/n2 exactly.

=== 0. THE ONE FACT SPECIFIC TO PROPORTIONS ===
For a Bernoulli variable the variance is a deterministic function of the mean: Var = mu(1-mu). Therefore H0: p1 = p2 IMPLIES equal variances, necessarily, not as an extra assumption. This is what licenses pooling here, and it is exactly what does not hold for general means -- for two arbitrary distributions, equal means do not imply equal variances (Behrens-Fisher), which is why the pooled/unpooled question does not even arise in the same form for a ratio-of-means derivation. Every argument below leans on this. Corollary that bites in practice: if the "binomial" metric is not one Bernoulli draw per randomization unit (e.g. conversion counted per session while randomization is per user), the variance is no longer v(p)/n, both SEs understate it, and none of this analysis is the binding problem.

=== 1. WHICH SE GOES WHERE -- ONE PRINCIPLE, NOT TWO ===
A confidence set is the inversion of a FAMILY of tests {H_d0 : delta = d0}. The score (Rao) test of H_d0 standardizes the score by the information evaluated at the NULL-CONSTRAINED maximum-likelihood estimate of the nuisance parameter. The p-value is the single member d0 = 0. Hence, from one principle:
  - p-value: the variance estimated under delta = 0. Under that constraint p1 = p2 and the constrained MLE of the common value is phat = (x1+x2)/(n1+n2). So SE_0 = sqrt( phat(1-phat)(1/n1 + 1/n2) ). This is Pearson's chi-square for the 2x2 table; Z_0^2 = chi^2_1 exactly.
  - interval: the variance estimated under EACH candidate d0, i.e. sigma_tilde(d0)^2 = v(ptilde1(d0))/n1 + v(ptilde2(d0))/n2 with ptilde2 - ptilde1 = d0. This is neither SE_0 nor SE_u. SE_u (the unpooled/Wald SE) is what you get by replacing the constrained MLE with the unconstrained one, which makes the SE independent of d0 and the interval symmetric.
So the correct statement is not "pooled for tests, unpooled for intervals". It is: pooled for the p-value because the p-value is the d0 = 0 member of the family; d0-dependent constrained SE for the interval because that is what inverting the family means; and the unpooled Wald interval is a legitimate but first-order approximation to the latter, obtained by freezing the constrained MLE at the unconstrained one.

Why the pooled SE is the better choice for the p-value specifically (three independent reasons): (a) it is the score statistic, and the score statistic is second-order accurate where the Wald statistic is only first-order, because the Wald statistic's SE is estimated at a point correlated with the numerator (section 7a); (b) under H0 the single nuisance parameter is estimated from all n1+n2 observations rather than from each arm separately, so the variance estimate is more efficient; (c) it coincides with the normal approximation to the conditional (Fisher) test, so it inherits that test's calibration.

=== 2. THE CONSTRAINED MLE, DERIVED ===
Maximize l = x1*log p1 + (n1-x1)*log(1-p1) + x2*log p2 + (n2-x2)*log(1-p2) subject to p2 = p1 + d. Write s = p1, t = s + d. Setting dl/ds = 0:
  x1/s - (n1-x1)/(1-s) + x2/t - (n2-x2)/(1-t) = 0.
Multiply by s(1-s)t(1-t) and group:
  [x1(1-s) - (n1-x1)s] * t(1-t) + [x2(1-t) - (n2-x2)t] * s(1-s) = 0,
and since x1(1-s) - (n1-x1)s = x1 - n1*s and likewise for arm 2, the constrained-MLE equation is simply
  (STAR)   (x1 - n1*s) * t(1-t) + (x2 - n2*t) * s(1-s) = 0,   t = s + d.
That is worth stating in that form: each arm contributes its own residual weighted by the OTHER arm's variance.

Expanding (STAR) with t = s + d gives a cubic in s (the quartic terms cancel):
  N*s^3 + [ (2*n1 + n2)*d - X - N ]*s^2 + [ X - (2*x1 + N)*d + n1*d^2 ]*s + x1*d*(1-d) = 0,   X = x1 + x2.
Check at d = 0: N*s^3 - (X+N)*s^2 + X*s = 0 => s*(N*s^2 - (X+N)*s + X) = 0 => s = 1 or s = X/N. The relevant root is the POOLED proportion, as it must be. That check is the cheapest guard against a mistyped coefficient.
The relevant root lies in [max(0,-d), min(1,1-d)]; Farrington-Manning (1990) give the standard trigonometric (Cardano) selection of it, so each evaluation of sigma_tilde(d) is O(1) with no iteration.

=== 3. IS THE POOLED-SE INTERVAL A CONFIDENCE SET? ===
Write SE_0^2 = v(pbar)*(1/n1 + 1/n2) with pbar = w*p1 + (1-w)*p2, and note 1/n1 + 1/n2 = 1/(N*w*(1-w)), and
  SE_u^2 = v(p1)/n1 + v(p2)/n2 = [ (1-w)*v(p1) + w*v(p2) ] / (N*w*(1-w)).
Note the REVERSED weights: the mean is weighted (w, 1-w), the variance combination (1-w, w). Hence
  SE_0^2 / SE_u^2 = v(pbar) / [ (1-w)v(p1) + w*v(p2) ]  =: A/B.
Expanding with p2 = p1 + d:
  A - B = (1-2w)(1-2*p1)*d + ( w - (1-w)^2 )*d^2.      (EXACT)
Balanced case w = 1/2: A - B = d^2/4 > 0 for every d != 0, so the pooled SE is ALWAYS the larger and the pooled interval is always conservative -- which is why the design is defensible-looking on balanced tests.
Imbalanced case: the LINEAR term dominates for |d| small, and its sign is (1-2w)(1-2p1)*sign(d). With w > 1/2 (control larger), p1 < 1/2 and d > 0 it is NEGATIVE: the pooled SE is SMALLER than the true one, i.e. the interval is too narrow.
Worked, checkable: n1 = 900, n2 = 100, x1 = 9, x2 = 2 (p1 = 0.01, p2 = 0.02). pbar = 11/1000 = 0.011; SE_0^2 = 0.011*0.989*(1/900+1/100) = 1.208778e-4; SE_u^2 = 0.01*0.99/900 + 0.02*0.98/100 = 1.1e-5 + 1.96e-4 = 2.07e-4. Ratio 0.5839, SE_0/SE_u = 0.7642. The EXACT identity reproduces the gap: A - B = (1-1.8)(1-0.02)(0.01) + (0.9 - 0.01)(1e-4) = -7.84e-3 + 8.9e-5 = -7.751e-3, divided by N*w*(1-w) = 90 gives -8.61e-5 = 1.2088e-4 - 2.07e-4. Confirmed.
Coverage consequence. The interval dhat +/- z*SE_0 covers delta iff |dhat - delta| <= z*SE_0. Asymptotically dhat - delta ~ N(0, SE_u_true^2) and SE_0 -> SE_0_true, so
  coverage -> 2*Phi( z * sqrt(A/B) ) - 1.
For the case above sqrt(A/B) = 0.764: a nominal 95% interval has asymptotic coverage 2*Phi(1.497)-1 = 86.6%; a nominal 99.6% (alpha = 0.004) interval has 2*Phi(2.199)-1 = 97.21%, i.e. a 2.79% error rate against a nominal 0.4% -- seven times nominal.
Limit w -> 1 (a tiny treatment arm against a huge control): A/B -> v(p1)/v(p2). With p1 = 0.001, p2 = 0.01 that is 0.101, sqrt = 0.318, and a nominal 95% interval has 46.6% coverage. In the other direction (p1 = 0.01, p2 = 0.001) A/B = 9.9 and the interval is 3.15x too wide.
THE POINT: A/B does not tend to 1 as n grows. The pooled variance estimate is INCONSISTENT for the variance of the quantity being bracketed whenever delta != 0. So the coverage does not converge to 1-alpha; the shortfall is a fixed function of (p1, p2, w). It is therefore not a confidence interval, asymptotically or otherwise. It is the acceptance region of the single test of delta = 0, plotted on the delta axis. At delta = 0 it is exactly right, which is why nothing about the false-positive rate ever complains.

=== 4. IS THE p<->CI EQUIVALENCE WORTH KEEPING? ===
With the pooled SE in both, "excludes 0" is |dhat| > z*SE_0 is "p < alpha" -- exactly, at every alpha, with no asymptotics. That equivalence is a genuinely desirable property. But it has been obtained by the one step that destroys the interval: freezing the d0 = 0 variance across all d0. Section 2 shows the same equivalence is available honestly -- invert the family, and the d0 = 0 member IS the p-value, so equality holds by construction while every other member uses its own correct variance. The discriminating question is which version survives perturbation: MN keeps the equivalence AND has correct coverage at every delta; the pooled interval keeps the equivalence by making every statement about a nonzero delta wrong. So: keep the property, replace the mechanism. And note the equivalence only ever concerned the single event "excludes zero". Everything else an interval is read for -- the magnitude, the precision claim, "the lift is at least X%", downstream meta-analysis, reading an achieved MDE back off the width -- is corrupted by the frozen variance, and by a factor that can reach 3x in width.

=== 5. THE SWITCH-THE-INTERVAL-ONLY CASE ===
See coherence_analysis; the algebra is: disagreement iff |dhat| lies between z*SE_0 and z*SE_u. R = SE_0/SE_u. Balanced: SE_0^2 - SE_u^2 = dhat^2 * (1/n1+1/n2)/4 = dhat^2/N, so at the boundary dhat ~ z*SE_u, R^2 = 1 + z^2/N and R - 1 ~ z^2/(2N). Imbalanced, for |d| << p so the linear term dominates and SE_u^2 ~ pq/(N w(1-w)): R^2 - 1 ~ (1-2w)(1-2p)*d/(pq); substituting the boundary value d = z*SE_u = z*sqrt(pq/(N w(1-w))) gives R^2 - 1 ~ -gamma_D*z, hence R ~ 1 - gamma_D*z/2 with gamma_D the skewness of section 6. The disagreement probability under H0 follows from shifting a normal threshold by z*|R-1|: 2*phi(z)*z*|R-1|.

=== 6. SKEWNESS OF THE DIFFERENCE, AND WHY BALANCE IS THE MASTER VARIABLE ===
Third cumulant of phat_j is v(p)(1-2p)/n_j^2, so under H0 (p1 = p2 = p)
  kappa_3(dhat) = v(p)(1-2p)*(1/n2^2 - 1/n1^2),   Var(dhat) = v(p)(1/n1 + 1/n2),
  gamma_D = kappa_3/Var^{3/2} = (1-2p)*(2w-1) / ( sqrt(N p q) * sqrt(w(1-w)) ).
Check: w = 1/2 gives exactly 0 -- the one-sample skewness of the two arms CANCELS under balance. Check: w -> 1 gives gamma_D -> (1-2p)/sqrt(n2 p q), the one-sample answer for the small arm. Both limits are right.
The same factor governs the Wald statistic's other defect: Cov(dhat, SEhat_u^2) = (1-2p)*v(p)*(1/n2^2 - 1/n1^2), again zero at w = 1/2.
STATEMENT WORTH REMEMBERING: under H0 with equal arm sizes, all the O(n^{-1/2}) terms vanish, and pooled vs unpooled, Wald vs score, Agresti-Caffo vs Wilson vs MN all agree to O(1/(n p q)). Everything that separates these methods is proportional either to the imbalance (2w-1) or to 1/(n p q). That is the single organizing fact of this whole analysis, and it says where to point the A/A instrument.

=== 7. WHY WALD COVERAGE IS POOR ===
(a) Variance-estimation correlation. The Wald SE is evaluated at phat, which is correlated with phat itself. One sample: Cov(phat, v(phat)/n) = (1-2p)v(p)/n^2, nonzero for every p != 1/2. For p < 1/2 a downward fluctuation of phat also shrinks the estimated SE, so the interval is short exactly when its centre is low -- systematic non-coverage on one side. This is Brown-Cai-DasGupta's diagnosis of the one-sample Wald interval and it is a first-order (O(n^{-1/2})) effect. For the two-sample DIFFERENCE the same covariance carries the factor (1/n2^2 - 1/n1^2), so balanced arms kill it. That is why the two-sample balanced Wald interval is far less bad than the one-sample Wald interval BCD indict, and why quoting their result as if it condemned this engine's balanced tests would be an overreach.
(b) Skewness and lattice. Edgeworth: for a standardized lattice sum, F(x) = Phi(x) - phi(x)*[ gamma(x^2-1)/6 + kappa4*(x^3-3x)/24 + gamma^2*(x^5-10x^3+15x)/72 ] + ... . For the UPPER tail alone the leading error is +phi(z)*gamma*(z^2-1)/6, and relative to the tail mass phi(z)/z that is gamma*z(z^2-1)/6. For a symmetric TWO-SIDED region the even skewness term cancels between the tails and the odd O(1/n) terms double, giving relative error ~ kappa4*z(z^3-3z)/24 + gamma^2*z(z^5-10z^3+15z)/72. Consequence to hold on to: a two-sided "excludes zero" decision enjoys the cancellation; a one-sided reading of a single endpoint ("the lift is at least L") does not, and is first-order wrong whenever the arms are imbalanced.
(c) Boundary collapse. x_j = 0 or n_j makes that arm's contribution to SE_u exactly zero; x1 = x2 = 0 makes the interval [0,0] -- a claim of infinite precision -- and makes the pooled statistic 0/0.

=== 8. WILSON, BY INVERSION ===
One sample. Invert the score test, i.e. solve (phat - p)^2 = z^2 * p(1-p)/n for p:
  n(phat-p)^2 = z^2 p(1-p)  =>  (n + z^2)p^2 - (2*n*phat + z^2)p + n*phat^2 = 0
  =>  p = [ phat + z^2/(2n) +/- z*sqrt( phat(1-phat)/n + z^2/(4n^2) ) ] / (1 + z^2/n).
The centre is ptilde = (x + z^2/2)/(n + z^2): the estimate shrunk toward 1/2 by z^2/2 pseudo-successes and z^2/2 pseudo-failures. The interval is symmetric about ptilde and therefore ASYMMETRIC about phat, with the asymmetry in the direction that matches the true skewness of phat. It never leaves [0,1] and never has zero width.
Is inverting the POOLED-SE test what yields it? One sample: yes -- the score test uses the NULL variance p0(1-p0)/n, and re-estimating it at every candidate p0 is exactly what produces the quadratic and hence the shrunk centre. Two samples: NO, and this is the most commonly conflated point in the whole subject. Inverting a test whose SE has been frozen at the delta0 = 0 (pooled) value produces the symmetric pooled-Wald interval and nothing Wilson-like at all -- the variance must be re-estimated under EACH delta0, which is section 2, i.e. Miettinen-Nurminen. "Pooled SE" is the value of the constrained-MLE variance at one point of the family, not the family.

=== 9. AGRESTI-CAFFO, DERIVED RATHER THAN ASSERTED ===
Section 8 gives the score centre (x + z^2/2)/(n + z^2). Agresti and Coull's one-sample proposal is to stop there and apply the WALD formula at the adjusted point; at z = 1.96, z^2/2 = 1.92 ~ 2, which is where "add two successes and two failures" comes from -- it is a rounding of z^2/2 at the 95% quantile. Agresti and Caffo (2000) carry the same idea to the two-sample difference by adding ONE success and ONE failure per arm (four pseudo-observations across the two arms, half of each type), i.e. ptilde_j = (x_j+1)/(n_j+2), then
  (ptilde2 - ptilde1) +/- z * sqrt( ptilde1(1-ptilde1)/(n1+2) + ptilde2(1-ptilde2)/(n2+2) ).
Where the "1" comes from: it is z^2/4 evaluated at z = 1.96 (= 0.96), the per-arm share of the score shrinkage when the total four pseudo-observations are split across two arms. The alpha-general form is therefore x_j + z^2/4 successes and z^2/4 failures, ntilde_j = n_j + z^2/2.
Two derived consequences the literature does not foreground, both testable: (i) the published constant is an alpha = 0.05 artifact. At alpha = 0.004, z^2/4 = 2.071, so the literal "+1" under-shrinks by a factor 2.07, and under-shrinking means an interval that is too narrow -- Agresti-Caffo as published is LIBERAL at small alpha in the sparse regime, which is the opposite of its reputation. (ii) The adjustment is O(1) added to n_j, so at n_j >= 1e4 it moves phat_j by <= 1e-4 absolute and the interval is numerically Wald. AC matters exactly and only where n*p is small -- an early cutoff, or a 1e-3 metric at the low end of the traffic range -- which happens to be where this engine's hard cases live.

=== 10. MIETTINEN-NURMINEN: WHAT IT BUYS AND COSTS ===
sigma_tilde(d)^2 = [ v(ptilde1)/n1 + v(ptilde2)/n2 ] * N/(N-1), with (ptilde1, ptilde2) from section 2; interval = {d : (dhat - d)^2 <= z^2 * sigma_tilde(d)^2}. Farrington-Manning is the same statistic without the N/(N-1) factor, which MN introduce as a small-sample bias correction of the variance estimate. At N >= 2e4 the factor is 1 + 5e-5.
Buys: exact coherence with the pooled p-value (Z(0) is identically the pooled statistic, because at d = 0 the constrained MLE of both arms is the pooled proportion -- see the d = 0 check under the cubic); bounds that are asymmetric in the direction the true sampling distribution is skewed; never zero width; always inside [-1,1]; correct behaviour under imbalance, because the variance is re-estimated at each candidate d instead of at pbar; and ONE principle that also generates the ratio interval (section 15) and the odds-ratio interval.
Costs: a bracketed root-find in d. Each evaluation is a cubic solve (closed form), so the cost is ~50 cubic solves per endpoint by bisection to double precision, or ~6 by Newton from a Wald start -- negligible against a warehouse query, but not free and not a one-liner. Z(d)^2 is smooth but not guaranteed unimodal for degenerate cells, so bracket over the whole feasible range with a coarse scan rather than trusting a local solver. And it is non-standard enough that a golden test must compare against an independent implementation (R "ratesci", SAS PROC FREQ RISKDIFF CL=MN), not against a second transcription of the same formula.
One honest caveat: the N/(N-1) factor is a heuristic, not a theorem. Applied to the interval only, it breaks the exact coherence by a relative 1/(2N). Apply it to both or to neither.

=== 11. NEWCOMBE HYBRID SCORE (his method 10) ===
Compute Wilson intervals (l_j, u_j) for each arm at level 1-alpha. Then
  L = dhat - sqrt( (phat2 - l2)^2 + (u1 - phat1)^2 ),   U = dhat + sqrt( (u2 - phat2)^2 + (phat1 - l1)^2 ).
Motivation: at the LOWER endpoint of the difference the relevant parameter values are a low p2 and a high p1, so the variance contribution of each arm is taken at its own score limit on that side, and the two half-widths are combined by squaring and adding (the variance of a difference of independent quantities). It is a "square-and-add of the two one-sample score intervals" and it is not the inversion of any single two-sample test.
Buys: closed form, no iteration, boundary-safe, coverage close to nominal across the parameter space (Newcombe 1998; Fagerland, Lydersen and Laake 2015 recommend it alongside MN). Costs: NO coherence with the pooled p-value -- "excludes zero" is not equivalent to any p one would print beside it; mild conservatism; and it inherits Wilson's boundary behaviour, whose conservatism grows without bound as alpha shrinks (section 13).

=== 12. CLOPPER-PEARSON, AND WHY IT IS THE WRONG DEFAULT HERE ===
CP is the one-sample exact interval {p : P_p(X >= x) >= alpha/2 and P_p(X <= x) >= alpha/2}, guaranteed coverage >= 1-alpha for every p by construction. Its two-sample analogues are the conditional exact (Fisher) interval or the unconditional exact intervals (Santner-Snell, Chan-Zhang, Agresti-Min), which require maximizing a tail probability over a nuisance parameter.
Why not here: (a) guaranteed coverage means strictly greater than 1-alpha almost everywhere, so the ACHIEVED level is well below alpha -- and the alpha budget has already been divided by 12; paying twice for conservatism is a power decision nobody consciously made. (b) The conservatism is worst exactly where the discreteness is worst, so it does not solve the sparse case, it only errs on the safe side of it. (c) Two-sample exact requires enumeration or a nuisance-parameter maximization per comparison per cutoff -- at n up to 1e7 that is a different order of computation from a cubic. (d) It is not coherent with the score p-value either, so it does not buy the property the pooled design was implicitly buying. Where it IS right: a single sparse safety metric, or a setting where exceeding alpha is categorically unacceptable.

=== 13. THE ZERO CELL AT SMALL ALPHA, EXACTLY ===
One sample, x = 0. Wilson upper bound = z^2/(n + z^2). Exact (CP) upper bound = 1 - (alpha/2)^{1/n} ~ ln(2/alpha)/n. At alpha = 0.05: 3.8415/n vs 3.689/n (+4%; this is the familiar "rule of three"). At alpha = 0.004: 8.2838/n vs 6.2146/n (+33%). As alpha -> 0, z^2 ~ 2*ln(1/alpha) while ln(2/alpha) ~ ln(1/alpha), so the ratio tends to 2: the score interval's zero-count bound is asymptotically TWICE the exact one. The direction is safe (conservative) but the conservatism is unbounded in alpha. Nobody reports this because coverage studies are run at alpha = 0.05.
Two-sample, x1 = x2 = 0, n1 = n2 = n. Solve (STAR): (0 - n*s)*t(1-t) + (0 - n*t)*s(1-s) = 0 => -n*s*t*[(1-t) + (1-s)] = 0 => s = 0 (with t = d). Then sigma_tilde^2 = 0 + d(1-d)/n and Z(d)^2 = n*d^2/(d(1-d)) = n*d/(1-d) = z^2 gives d = z^2/(n + z^2). So the MN/score interval at a double-zero table is exactly +/- z^2/(n+z^2) -- the Wilson zero bound, symmetrically. The Wald interval at the same table is [0, 0]. This is the cleanest single demonstration of the difference and makes an ideal known-answer test.

=== 14. SMALL ALPHA ===
See the dedicated field; the three channels are (i) the Edgeworth tail-shape error, (ii) the lattice attainability floor, (iii) the exponential sensitivity of a tail probability to a mis-scaled SE, which is the master law: if the reported SE is r times the true one, the achieved error rate is inflated by (1/r)*exp( z^2 (1 - r^2)/2 ). For r = 1 - e with small e that is ~ exp(z^2 * e): the penalty for a wrong SE grows like the SQUARE of the quantile in the exponent, so a 5% SE error costs 21% extra false positives at alpha = 0.05 and 51% at alpha = 0.004.

=== 15. THE RELATIVE FORM ===
See the dedicated field. Headline: derive it on its own scale by the same score inversion. The constrained MLE under p2 = theta*p1 follows from the same multiply-through trick: (x1 - n1*s)(1 - theta*s) + (x2 - n2*theta*s)(1 - s) = 0, i.e. the QUADRATIC
  N*theta*s^2 - [ theta*(x1 + n2) + (n1 + x2) ]*s + X = 0,   s = ptilde1, ptilde2 = theta*ptilde1,
with the root s = [B - sqrt(B^2 - 4*N*theta*X)]/(2*N*theta), B = theta(x1+n2) + (n1+x2). At theta = 1 this reduces to N*s^2 - (X+N)*s + X = 0, root X/N -- the pooled proportion again -- and the statistic Z(theta) = (phat2 - theta*phat1)/sqrt( theta^2*v(ptilde1)/n1 + v(ptilde2)/n2 ) becomes at theta = 1 exactly the pooled two-sample z. Hence the ratio interval excludes 1 iff the difference interval excludes 0 iff p < alpha: three-way coherence from one principle.

recommended.name: Score-test inversion with constrained-MLE variance (Miettinen-Nurminen 1985; the uncorrected form is Farrington-Manning 1990), used as a single statistic for the p-value, the absolute interval and the relative interval
recommended.interval: { d in [-1,1] : (phat2 - phat1 - d)^2 <= z^2 * sigma_tilde(d)^2 }, where sigma_tilde(d)^2 = [ ptilde1(1-ptilde1)/n1 + ptilde2(1-ptilde2)/n2 ] * N/(N-1), ptilde2 = ptilde1 + d, and ptilde1 is the root in [max(0,-d), min(1,1-d)] of the cubic N*s^3 + [(2*n1+n2)*d - X - N]*s^2 + [X - (2*x1+N)*d + n1*d^2]*s + x1*d*(1-d) = 0 (X = x1+x2, N = n1+n2). Endpoints by bracketed root-find on Z(d)^2 - z^2 over a scan of [-1,1] (or a Newton iteration started from the Wald endpoints). Bounds are asymmetric about the point estimate and must be reported as [L, U], never as '+/-'.
recommended.pvalue: 2*(1 - Phi(|Z(0)|)) with Z(0) = (phat2 - phat1)/sqrt( phat*(1-phat)*(1/n1 + 1/n2) * N/(N-1) ), phat = (x1+x2)/N. Without the N/(N-1) factor this is exactly the classical pooled two-sample z and Z(0)^2 is exactly Pearson's chi-square for the 2x2 table; with it, it is the d=0 member of the same family as the interval. Apply the factor in both places or in neither. Define x1=x2=0 (and x1=n1, x2=n2) as p = 1 rather than 0/0.
recommended.rationale: It answers the coherence question and the validity question with one object instead of trading them off. The p-value is unchanged from the classical pooled test (so no reported p moves, up to the optional 5e-5 factor), the interval becomes a genuine confidence set at every value of the difference rather than only at zero, the boundary cases stop being special cases (a double-zero table yields +/- z^2/(n+z^2), not [0,0]), the interval respects [-1,1] and is asymmetric in the direction the sampling distribution actually is, and imbalanced designs -- where every defect in this analysis concentrates -- are handled by construction because the variance is re-estimated under each candidate difference instead of frozen at the pooled value. The cost is a bracketed root-find over a closed-form cubic: order 50 cubic solves per endpoint, which is nothing beside the warehouse read that produced x1, n1, x2, n2. Fagerland, Lydersen and Laake (2015) recommend MN and Newcombe's hybrid score as the two intervals for two independent proportions; MN is the one of the two that is coherent with the printed p-value.
recommended.preserves_coherence: Exactly, and by construction rather than by coincidence: the interval is the set of d not rejected by the family whose d = 0 member IS the p-value, so 'the interval excludes zero' and 'p < alpha' are the same event at every alpha, at every sample size, with no asymptotics -- while the interval remains valid at nonzero d, which is precisely what the pooled-SE interval sacrificed to get the same equality. Two implementation conditions: (a) use the same N/(N-1) convention in both, or the equality is broken by a relative 1/(2N); (b) compute the reject flag from the interval OR from the p-value but derive both from the one Z, so that floating-point rounding at the exact boundary cannot produce a disagreement the mathematics forbids. The same construction on the ratio scale (constrained MLE under p2 = theta*p1) has Z(1) identically equal to Z(0) of the difference scale, so the relative interval's exclusion of 1 is the same event too -- three-way coherence.

alternatives.name: Wald / unpooled (the status-quo-shaped interval beside a pooled p-value)
alternatives.coverage_behaviour: First-order correct at every delta, so unlike the pooled-SE interval it IS a confidence interval asymptotically. Its errors: (a) the SE is evaluated at a point correlated with the centre, Cov(dhat, SEhat^2) = (1-2p)v(p)(1/n2^2 - 1/n1^2), which is first-order in 1/sqrt(n) under imbalance and exactly zero under balance; (b) skewness gamma_D = (1-2p)(2w-1)/(sqrt(Npq)sqrt(w(1-w))), again zero under balance -- and for a two-sided decision the skewness term cancels between the tails, leaving O(1/(npq)); (c) it collapses to zero width when x_j hits 0 or n_j and can then exclude zero spuriously or claim infinite precision. Practical summary: on balanced non-sparse comparisons it is numerically indistinguishable from MN (relative difference O(z^2/N) ~ 2e-4); on imbalanced or sparse ones it is the worst of the honest options.
alternatives.when_preferable: When a closed form with no root-finding is mandatory, arms are within a few percent of balanced, min(n_j*p_j, n_j*q_j) is comfortably above the section-14 thresholds, and the incoherence with a pooled p-value is either accepted and displayed or removed by also switching the p-value to unpooled (which costs test accuracy -- not recommended).

alternatives.name: Agresti-Caffo (alpha-general form)
alternatives.formula: ptilde_j = (x_j + z^2/4)/(n_j + z^2/2); interval = (ptilde2 - ptilde1) +/- z * sqrt( ptilde1(1-ptilde1)/(n1 + z^2/2) + ptilde2(1-ptilde2)/(n2 + z^2/2) ). The published '+1 success, +1 failure per arm' is this with z^2/4 rounded at z = 1.96.
alternatives.coverage_behaviour: Mimics the score interval's shrinkage without its root-find; coverage close to nominal at alpha = 0.05 across the parameter space and dramatically better than Wald near the boundaries (Agresti-Caffo 2000). Two derived limitations: the pseudo-count is calibrated at z = 1.96, so the literal '+1' under-shrinks by z^2/4 = 2.07 at alpha = 0.004 and the interval is then too narrow (liberal) in the sparse regime -- use z^2/4, not 1; and the adjustment is O(1) added to n_j, so at n_j >= 1e4 with n_j*p_j >> 1 it is numerically identical to Wald and buys nothing.
alternatives.when_preferable: As the cheap closed-form default when root-finding is genuinely off the table: it is boundary-safe, it degrades gracefully, and with the z^2/4 correction it has no alpha-specific failure mode. It is still incoherent with the pooled p-value.

alternatives.name: Newcombe hybrid score (method 10)
alternatives.formula: With (l_j, u_j) the Wilson intervals per arm at level 1-alpha: L = dhat - sqrt((phat2-l2)^2 + (u1-phat1)^2), U = dhat + sqrt((u2-phat2)^2 + (phat1-l1)^2).
alternatives.coverage_behaviour: Coverage close to nominal over the whole parameter space including small n and boundary cells (Newcombe 1998); recommended alongside MN by Fagerland et al. (2015). Mildly conservative. Inherits Wilson's zero-cell behaviour, whose conservatism relative to the exact bound grows without bound as alpha shrinks (ratio -> 2). Not the inversion of any single test, so 'excludes zero' corresponds to no printable p-value.
alternatives.when_preferable: When a closed form is required AND boundary robustness matters more than coherence -- e.g. a sparse guardrail metric reported without a p-value, or a second opinion used to audit MN's root-find.

alternatives.name: Pooled SE in both the p-value and the interval (perfect coherence, invalid interval)
alternatives.coverage_behaviour: Exact coverage 1-alpha at delta = 0 only. For delta != 0 the asymptotic coverage is 2*Phi(z*sqrt(A/B)) - 1 with A/B = v(pbar)/[(1-w)v(p1) + w*v(p2)], which does not tend to 1 as n grows: the variance estimator is inconsistent for the variance of the quantity being bracketed. Balanced arms make it conservative (A - B = d^2/4 > 0 always). Imbalanced arms can make it anticonservative: n1=900, n2=100, p1=0.01, p2=0.02 gives width ratio 0.764 and nominal-95% coverage 86.6% (nominal-99.6% coverage 97.2%, i.e. seven times the intended error rate); in the limit of an extreme holdout with a 10x rate gap it reaches 46.6% coverage at nominal 95%. Its false-positive rate, however, is exactly the pooled test's and therefore perfectly calibrated -- which is why an A/A false-positive measurement can never see the defect.
alternatives.when_preferable: Never as a confidence interval. It is defensible only if relabelled as what it is -- the acceptance region of the test of delta = 0 -- and if nothing downstream reads it as a precision statement. Since a report that prints an effect with an interval is exactly a precision statement, that condition is not satisfiable in this engine.

alternatives.name: Clopper-Pearson (one-sample) / exact unconditional two-sample (Santner-Snell, Chan-Zhang, Agresti-Min)
alternatives.formula: One sample: {p : P_p(X >= x) >= alpha/2 and P_p(X <= x) >= alpha/2}, i.e. Beta(x, n-x+1) and Beta(x+1, n-x) quantiles. Two samples: invert the exact test, maximizing the tail probability over the nuisance parameter at each candidate delta.
alternatives.coverage_behaviour: Coverage >= 1-alpha guaranteed for every parameter value and every alpha -- the only candidate with no asymptotic assumption to fail. The price is that coverage strictly exceeds 1-alpha almost everywhere; in the sparse regime the achieved error rate can be a small fraction of nominal, so the power loss compounds with an alpha already divided by the multiplicity correction. Computationally the two-sample version needs enumeration or a nuisance maximization per comparison.
alternatives.when_preferable: A single sparse safety/guardrail metric where exceeding alpha is categorically unacceptable and power is secondary; or as the arbiter in a known-answer test at tiny n where the asymptotic candidates are all suspect.

small_alpha_regime:
Coverage papers report alpha = 0.05; this engine runs at 0.004 and below, so the alpha-dependence has to be derived, not extrapolated. There are THREE distinct channels and they scale differently in z = z_{1-alpha/2}. Recall z ~ sqrt(2*ln(1/alpha)), so every z^k law is a (ln 1/alpha)^{k/2} law in alpha -- mild in alpha, but the constants are what bite.

CHANNEL 1 -- SENSITIVITY TO A MIS-SCALED SE (the master law, and the one that matters most). If the reported SE is r times the true one, the achieved two-sided error rate is inflated by the factor Phibar(z*r)/Phibar(z) ~ (1/r)*exp( z^2 (1-r^2)/2 ), using Phibar(x) ~ phi(x)/x. For r = 1-e with e small this is ~ exp(z^2 * e). So the tolerance on the SE for a fixed inflation scales as 1/z^2. Numbers: a 1% SE understatement inflates the error rate by 3.9% at alpha = 0.05 (z^2 = 3.84) and by 8.7% at alpha = 0.004 (z^2 = 8.28); a 5% understatement, by 21% and 51% respectively; at alpha = 1e-4 (z = 3.891, z^2 = 15.14) a 5% understatement costs 108%. And for the pooled-SE interval with r = 0.764 (the 900/100 example) the inflation is 2.7x at alpha = 0.05, 7.0x at alpha = 0.004 and 30x at alpha = 1e-4: the RELATIVE damage of a wrong SE scale grows without bound as alpha shrinks, exponentially in z^2. This is the sharpest small-alpha statement in the whole analysis and it is method-agnostic.

CHANNEL 2 -- TAIL-SHAPE (EDGEWORTH) ERROR of the normal approximation. Two-sided, the skewness term cancels between the tails and the O(1/n) odd terms double, giving relative error ~ kappa4hat*z(z^3-3z)/24 + gammahat^2*z(z^5-10z^3+15z)/72. For BALANCED arms gammahat = 0 exactly and kappa4hat = (1-6pq)/(2*n*p*q) with n per arm, so
  relative error ~ (1-6pq) * (z^4 - 3z^2) / (48 * n * p * q).
Requiring <= 10%: n*p*q >= (z^4 - 3z^2)/4.8. Table: z = 1.960 (alpha .05) -> 0.7; z = 2.878 (alpha .004) -> 9.1; z = 3.891 (alpha 1e-4) -> 38; z = 4.417 (alpha 1e-5) -> 67. Asymptotically npq ~ z^4. Mild -- balanced two-sample proportions are well behaved.
For IMBALANCED arms, or for any ONE-SIDED reading (a single endpoint, "the lift is at least L"), the skewness term survives: relative error ~ gamma_D*z(z^2-1)/6 with gamma_D = (1-2p)(2w-1)/(sqrt(N p q) sqrt(w(1-w))). Requiring <= 10%: N*p*q >= [ (1-2p)|2w-1| z(z^2-1) / (0.6 * sqrt(w(1-w))) ]^2, asymptotically ~ z^6. At an 80/20 split (|2w-1|/sqrt(w(1-w)) = 1.5) and p small: z = 1.96 -> Npq >= 194; z = 2.878 -> 2747; z = 3.891 -> 18879. Going from alpha = 0.05 to alpha = 0.004 multiplies the requirement by 14.2 (the asymptotic z^6 ratio is 10.0; the finite-z ratio is larger because z(z^2-1) is not yet z^3). At p = 0.01 that means N >= 2.8e5 for a 10%-accurate one-sided tail at alpha = 0.004 -- inside the stated traffic range, but above its low end.
SO: THE ANSWER TO "HOW DOES REQUIRED np SCALE WITH z" IS NOT ONE NUMBER. Two-sided and balanced: npq ~ z^4. One-sided or imbalanced: npq ~ z^6. Attainability floor: npq ~ z^2 (channel 3). And the tolerance on the SE itself, channel 1, scales as 1/z^2.

CHANNEL 3 -- DISCRETENESS, WHICH IS A FLOOR NO METHOD BEATS. The support of dhat is a lattice; with n1 = n2 = n the step is 1/n, which in standardized units is delta_step = (1/n)/sqrt(2pq/n) = 1/sqrt(2*n*p*q). Since d/dz log(tail) ~ -z, one lattice step changes the tail probability by a relative ~ z*delta_step = z/sqrt(2npq). Requiring the granularity of the ATTAINABLE level to be <= 10%: npq >= z^2/(2*0.01) = 50*z^2. Table: z = 1.96 -> 192; z = 2.878 -> 414; z = 3.891 -> 757; z = 4.417 -> 976. At p = 1e-3 that is n >= 4.1e5 per arm at alpha = 0.004 -- i.e. the low end of the stated traffic range (1e4) is nowhere near it. Concrete anchor: Bin(1e4, 1e-3) ~ Poisson(10); P(X >= 21) = 0.0035 and P(X >= 22) = 0.0016. The attainable one-sided levels near 0.002 differ by more than a factor of two, so a nominal alpha = 0.004 is simply NOT ATTAINABLE by any non-randomized rule at that npq. What one can choose is the DIRECTION of the miss: exact methods land above nominal coverage (conservative), score methods land near it and oscillate, Wald lands below. Two mitigations exist and both cost something: mid-p (gives up guaranteed validity for granularity) and randomized tests (nobody will accept them). The convolution of two independent binomials smooths the lattice somewhat -- markedly so when n1 != n2, since the support of x2/n2 - x1/n1 is then much finer than 1/n -- which is one of the very few respects in which imbalance helps.

METHOD-SPECIFIC ALPHA ARTEFACTS. (a) Agresti-Caffo's "+1 success, +1 failure per arm" is z^2/4 at z = 1.96; at alpha = 0.004 the correct count is 2.07, so the published constant under-shrinks by 2.1x and the interval is too narrow in the sparse regime -- a liberal failure at small alpha, opposite to AC's reputation. (b) Wilson's zero-count upper bound is z^2/(n+z^2) against the exact 1-(alpha/2)^{1/n} ~ ln(2/alpha)/n; the ratio is 1.04 at alpha = 0.05, 1.27 at alpha = 0.004 (finite n = 100), and tends to z^2/ln(1/alpha) -> 2 as alpha -> 0. Conservative, unbounded, and inherited by Newcombe. (c) MN/score has no alpha-calibrated constant at all -- its shape is derived at whatever z is supplied -- which is the structural reason to prefer it in a system whose alpha is set by a multiplicity correction rather than by convention. (d) The pooled-SE interval's error is alpha-independent at delta = 0 by construction and grows exponentially in z^2 as a multiple of nominal at delta != 0 (channel 1).
boundary_cases: x1 = x2 = 0 (or x1 = n1 and x2 = n2). The pooled statistic is 0/0 and the Wald interval is exactly [0, 0] -- a zero-width interval asserting infinite precision, which will also compare as 'does not exclude zero' only by luck of the inequality's strictness. The score/MN interval is well defined: solving (x1 - n1*s)t(1-t) + (x2 - n2*t)s(1-s) = 0 at x1 = x2 = 0 gives ptilde1 = 0, ptilde2 = d, hence Z(d)^2 = n*d/(1-d) for n1 = n2 = n, so the interval is exactly +/- z^2/(n+z^2) -- the Wilson zero bound. Required engine behaviour: define the p-value as 1 (not NaN, not 0), the effect as 0, and still report a real interval.

x_j = 0 in ONE arm only. Wald contributes zero variance from that arm, so the interval is too narrow on the side that matters and can exclude zero on the strength of the other arm alone. The relative effect is 0 or infinite and log-RR is -inf, so any delta-method ratio interval is undefined. Score/MN and Newcombe are finite and correct. This is the common case at an early cutoff on a 1e-3 metric, not an exotic one.

Small p with large n, i.e. n*p of order 10-100 at an early cutoff. The smooth Edgeworth error is tolerable (npq >= 9 for a 10%-accurate two-sided tail at alpha = 0.004 under balance) but the ATTAINABILITY floor is not: npq >= 414 is needed for 10% granularity, and at npq = 10 the achievable levels near alpha/2 = 0.002 jump by more than a factor of two. Required engine behaviour: this is not a method choice, it is a disclosure -- at these counts no interval and no p-value is accurate to the nominal alpha, and the honest options are to widen (exact/score) and to say so, or to suppress the verdict until npq crosses a stated threshold.

Strong arm-size imbalance (holdouts of 90/10, 95/5, 99/1). This is where EVERY separation in this analysis lives: the pooled-vs-unpooled SE gap is linear in the effect rather than quadratic (and can make the pooled SE the SMALLER one, so the pooled interval becomes anticonservative rather than conservative); the skewness gamma_D is proportional to (2w-1)/sqrt(w(1-w)) and is exactly zero at balance; the Wald SE's correlation with its own centre carries the same factor; and the p-value/interval disagreement rate rises from ~1e-5 to ~1e-3 per comparison. Effective sample size is the harmonic one -- 1/n1 + 1/n2 is dominated by the smaller arm -- so a 99/1 split with 1e6 total units behaves like a balanced test with 2e4.
n_j = 0, or a variant with no exposed units at an early cutoff. Every formula divides by n_j. Must be a defined refusal, not a NaN that propagates into a persisted interval.

phat exactly 0.5 in an arm, or p1 = p2 exactly. Harmless but worth a test: the linear imbalance term carries (1-2p1) and vanishes at p1 = 0.5, so a test fixture built at p = 0.5 will show NO pooled/unpooled separation regardless of imbalance and will silently certify nothing.

dhat at or beyond the feasible boundary: any interval endpoint must be clipped to [-1, 1] for the difference and [0, inf) for the ratio. Wald and pooled-Wald both violate this routinely at small n; score/MN cannot, by construction.

A cutoff where the two arms have identical rates (x1/n1 = x2/n2 exactly). Z = 0, and the MN interval about a zero point estimate is symmetric only if n1 = n2; with n1 != n2 it is NOT symmetric, which will look like a bug to anyone expecting '+/-'. Worth a test so nobody 'fixes' it.
relative_form:
The relative effect is rho = (p2 - p1)/p1 = RR - 1. Three routes; only one of them is coherent, and the specifically-proportions content is in why.

ROUTE A (divide the difference interval by phat1): wrong, and not by a subtlety. It treats phat1 as known, so it omits the denominator's sampling error entirely; it can produce rho < -1, which is impossible; and it corresponds to the inversion of no test, so its exclusion of zero matches neither the p-value nor the difference interval except by the accident of a positive divisor.

ROUTE B (delta method on the log): Var(log RRhat) ~ q1/(n1 p1) + q2/(n2 p2), estimated as (1-phat1)/x1 + (1-phat2)/x2, which for small p is ~ 1/x1 + 1/x2. Interval: exp( log RRhat +/- z*sqrt(1/x1 + 1/x2) ), then subtract 1. THIS IS WHERE THE PROPORTION-SPECIFIC STRUCTURE SHOWS. For a general positive mean the log-scale variance is sigma^2/(n mu^2) with sigma^2 a free parameter; for a Bernoulli, sigma^2 = p(1-p) is TIED to the mean, so the log-scale variance is q/(np) exactly. Three consequences a ratio-of-general-means derivation cannot give you: (i) the width depends on the COUNTS only, not on n -- half-width = z*sqrt(1/x1 + 1/x2) to leading order -- so ten times the traffic at a ten times smaller rate buys exactly nothing; (ii) the variance vanishes as p -> 1, so the relative effect on a high-rate metric is estimated far more precisely than the absolute one, the reverse of the usual intuition; (iii) it is undefined at x_j = 0, which a live engine hits. Quotable precision law: for +/- 10% relative precision on RR at alpha = 0.004 you need z*sqrt(1/x1 + 1/x2) <= 0.1, i.e. 1/x1 + 1/x2 <= 1.208e-3, i.e. about 1657 CONVERSIONS per arm (not units). Below a few hundred conversions per arm the relative effect is essentially unidentified: at x1 = x2 = 10 the interval is [0.28*RRhat, 3.6*RRhat].
The log transform is also better behaved than the raw ratio scale for small p (it pulls the long right tail in), so Route B is a real improvement on "ratio plus symmetric error bars" -- it just is not coherent with the difference interval or the p-value.

ROUTE C (RECOMMENDED -- invert the score test on the ratio scale, the same principle as the difference). Constrain p2 = theta*p1 and maximize the likelihood. The same multiply-through as (STAR) gives (x1 - n1*s)(1 - theta*s) + (x2 - n2*theta*s)(1 - s) = 0, a QUADRATIC (not a cubic):
  N*theta*s^2 - [ theta*(x1 + n2) + (n1 + x2) ]*s + X = 0,   ptilde1 = [B - sqrt(B^2 - 4*N*theta*X)]/(2*N*theta), B = theta(x1+n2) + (n1+x2), ptilde2 = theta*ptilde1.
Statistic: Z(theta) = (phat2 - theta*phat1) / sqrt( theta^2 * ptilde1(1-ptilde1)/n1 + ptilde2(1-ptilde2)/n2 ), optionally times the N/(N-1) correction; interval = {theta : Z(theta)^2 <= z^2}; report rho in [theta_L - 1, theta_U - 1]. (Miettinen-Nurminen 1985; equivalently Koopman 1984, Nam 1995, Gart-Nam 1988.)
TWO PROPERTIES THAT SETTLE THE QUESTION. (1) At theta = 1 the quadratic becomes N*s^2 - (X+N)*s + X = 0 with root X/N -- the pooled proportion -- and Z(1) is IDENTICALLY the pooled two-sample z, the same number as Z(0) on the difference scale. Therefore the relative interval excludes 0 iff the absolute interval excludes 0 iff p < alpha. Three surfaces, one decision, no possibility of a report that says "the lift is between -1% and +4%" beside "p = 0.002". Route A and Route B both fail this. (2) The construction is exactly equivariant under swapping the arms: relabelling sends theta -> 1/theta, and one checks that the numerator becomes -(1/theta)(phat2 - theta*phat1) while sigma_tilde becomes sigma_tilde/theta, so |Z| is unchanged and the interval maps to its reciprocal. A delta-method-on-log interval has this property only approximately; Route A does not have it at all.
Route C also survives x2 = 0 (finite upper bound, lower bound 0) where Route B is -inf, and it never produces rho < -1. Costs: a root-find in theta over (0, inf) -- bracket on the log scale, since the interval is naturally multiplicative -- plus care that theta_L is searched down to 0 when x2 = 0.
Display rule regardless of route: the relative interval is intrinsically asymmetric about rhohat and must be rendered as [L, U], never as "rhohat +/- h".

known_answer_tests.setup: x1 = x2 = 0, n1 = n2 = 1000, alpha = 0.05 (z = 1.9599640). Compute the difference interval by each candidate.
known_answer_tests.expected: Score/MN (without the N/(N-1) factor) gives EXACTLY +/- z^2/(n + z^2) = 3.8414588/1003.8414588 = +/- 0.00382670. Wald gives [0, 0]. Pooled-SE gives [0, 0]. Agresti-Caffo (z^2/4 = 0.960 pseudo-successes per arm) gives a small but nonzero width. The p-value must be reported as 1, not NaN.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It separates every candidate at once with a single table, it has a closed-form answer derived from the constrained-MLE equation rather than quoted, and it is the exact table a sparse metric produces at its first cutoff. Any implementation that special-cases 'zero variance' will return something else.

known_answer_tests.setup: Any (x1, n1, x2, n2). Solve the constrained-MLE cubic N*s^3 + [(2n1+n2)d - X - N]s^2 + [X - (2x1+N)d + n1 d^2]s + x1 d(1-d) = 0 at d = 0.
known_answer_tests.expected: The roots are s = 0, s = 1 and s = X/N; the admissible one is exactly the pooled proportion (x1+x2)/(n1+n2), and sigma_tilde(0)^2 is then exactly the pooled SE^2.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is the cheapest possible guard against a mistyped cubic coefficient, and it is the algebraic statement of the coherence property -- if this check fails, the interval and the p-value are silently different statistics.

known_answer_tests.setup: n1 = 900, n2 = 100, x1 = 9, x2 = 2. Compute SE_0^2 and SE_u^2.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It falsifies the widespread belief that the pooled SE is always the conservative one (true only at w = 1/2, where SE_0^2 - SE_u^2 = (d^2/4)(1/n1+1/n2) > 0). Here the pooled interval is 24% too NARROW. Any documentation claiming pooled is safe should fail this test.

known_answer_tests.setup: Coherence sweep: for a grid of tables spanning p in {1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1, 0.5}, w in {0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.99}, alpha in {0.05, 0.004, 1e-4}, compute the MN p-value and the MN interval with the SAME N/(N-1) convention, and check the two verdicts.
known_answer_tests.expected: Zero disagreements, at every point, to floating-point rounding at the exact boundary. If the factor is applied only to the interval, disagreements appear at a relative distance 1/(2N) from the boundary and only there.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is the property the whole recommendation exists to buy, and it is the one that silently breaks if a later change applies a correction factor to one side only.

known_answer_tests.setup: Zero-cell bound vs alpha: n = 100, x = 0. Compare the Wilson upper bound z^2/(n+z^2) with the exact Clopper-Pearson upper bound 1 - (alpha/2)^{1/n}.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It makes the small-alpha degradation of score intervals concrete and directional (conservative), and it will catch any implementation that hard-codes a 'rule of three' style bound calibrated at 95%.

known_answer_tests.setup: Agresti-Caffo pseudo-count: n_j = 200, x_j = 2, alpha = 0.004. Compare ptilde with the published +1 and with the alpha-general z^2/4 = 2.0710.
known_answer_tests.expected: 3/202 = 0.0148515 versus 4.0710/204.142 = 0.0199420 -- a 34% difference in the point at which the variance is evaluated, and correspondingly narrower vs wider intervals.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It exposes the hidden alpha = 0.05 calibration inside a constant that looks like a universal rule, in exactly the sparse regime where AC is the reason one would use AC at all.

known_answer_tests.setup: Ratio-scale arm-swap equivariance: for several tables compute the MN ratio interval [theta_L, theta_U] for (arm1, arm2) and [theta_L', theta_U'] for the swapped labelling.
known_answer_tests.expected: theta_L' = 1/theta_U and theta_U' = 1/theta_L, exactly (the algebra: swapping sends the numerator to -(1/theta) times the original and sigma_tilde to sigma_tilde/theta, so |Z| is invariant).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: It is a property Route A does not have at all and Route B has only to first order; it is also a cheap detector of a sign or index error in the constrained-MLE quadratic.

discriminating_predictions: RESOLUTION LAW FIRST, so every prediction below can be read against it. From M placebo iterations the 2-sigma resolution on a measured FPR is 2*sqrt(alpha(1-alpha)/M) ~ 2*sqrt(alpha/M). If the harness sizes iterations as M = c/alpha, the resolvable difference is 2*alpha/sqrt(c) -- a FIXED relative resolution of 2/sqrt(c), independent of alpha. [Contamination: I know from injected material that this harness uses c = 200, giving a 14% relative floor; the law itself is derived here.] So: an FPR difference smaller than about 14% of alpha is INVISIBLE to this instrument at its default iteration count, whatever alpha is.

BALANCED PLACEBO SPLIT, npq >= 1e3: pooled-SE, unpooled Wald, Agresti-Caffo(z^2/4), Newcombe and MN all produce the same decision on all but O(z^2/N) of iterations, so their measured FPRs agree to |dFPR|/alpha < 1e-3. Resolving that needs M ~ 4/(1e-6 * alpha) ~ 1e9 iterations. PREDICTION: the A/A FPR column CANNOT arbitrate the pooled-vs-unpooled question on balanced splits at any feasible cost. A run that reports a difference there is reporting Monte-Carlo noise or a bug.

IMBALANCED PLACEBO SPLIT is where the instrument can see. Configure the placebo permutation at 80/20 with p ~ 0.01 and N ~ 1e5 (small arm still has ~200 conversions -- nothing sparse). Add ONE new column: the fraction of placebo iterations on which 'interval excludes zero' and 'p < alpha' disagree. PREDICTION: pooled-both = exactly 0; MN = exactly 0; pooled-p + unpooled-Wald-CI = 2*phi(z)*z*|1-R| with |1-R| ~ gamma_D*z/2 = 0.067, i.e. 2.4e-3 per iteration. At M = 5e4 that is ~120 events, measurable to 10%. At a balanced split the same column reads ~7.6e-6, i.e. 0-1 events in 5e4 -- the same experiment run balanced proves nothing.

IMBALANCED AND SPARSE (n_small * p ~ 20-50, 90/10 split): PREDICTION on the ORDERING of measured FPR/alpha, which is more robust than any single value -- unpooled Wald > 1 (liberal), pooled/score ~ 1, published Agresti-Caffo (+1) slightly below Wald but still possibly > 1 at alpha = 0.004 because the pseudo-count is under-scaled by 2.07x, alpha-general Agresti-Caffo (z^2/4) < 1, Newcombe < 1, exact << 1. If the measured ordering differs, the placebo cohort is not behaving as independent Bernoulli units (check for multi-event units before blaming the method).

ALPHA SWEEP AT FIXED COHORT, BALANCED: measure FPR at alpha in {0.05, 0.01, 0.004, 0.001} and plot (FPR/alpha - 1) against (z^4 - 3z^2). PREDICTION: a straight line through the origin with slope (1-6pq)/(48*n*p*q). A slope materially steeper than that indicts the SE or the cohort (overdispersion), not the normal tail. This is a cheap self-test of the instrument before it is used to arbitrate anything.

COVERAGE UNDER AN INJECTED EFFECT IS THE COLUMN THAT CONDEMNS THE POOLED INTERVAL, AND THE ONLY ONE. Inject a known delta on an IMBALANCED split -- e.g. w = 0.9, p1 = 0.01, p2 = 0.02 -- and measure the fraction of iterations whose interval covers the injected delta. PREDICTION, computable in closed form BEFORE the run from 2*Phi(z*sqrt(A/B))-1 with A/B = v(pbar)/[(1-w)v(p1)+w*v(p2)] = 0.5839: nominal 95% -> 86.6% coverage; nominal 99.6% -> 97.2% coverage. Every other candidate lands within Monte-Carlo error of nominal. M = 400 iterations already resolves an 8-point coverage gap, so this is the cheapest decisive experiment in the whole set.

EXAGGERATION / TYPE-M IS PREDICTED TO BE UNCHANGED by the SE choice, because the point estimate phat2 - phat1 is identical across all candidates and only the selection event differs. PREDICTION: any measured exaggeration difference between pooled and unpooled intervals is a second-order artefact of the changed selection boundary and should be at most O(|1-R|) in magnitude. If the harness reports a large difference, it is measuring something else (e.g. conditioning on a decision computed by a different rule than the one whose estimates it averages).

ZERO-CELL LEG: seed the placebo cohort so that p ~ 3/n and a material fraction of iterations produce x_j = 0 in one arm. PREDICTION: the Wald and pooled-Wald rules produce zero-width or spuriously-excluding intervals on those iterations at a rate that shows up directly in the FPR column (gross, not subtle); MN, Newcombe and AC do not. This is the one boundary defect the instrument sees easily and cheaply.

WHERE THE INSTRUMENT IS STRUCTURALLY BLIND -- state these before running anything. (a) The pooled interval's invalidity is invisible to ANY A/A false-positive measurement, because a label permutation forces delta = 0 exactly, and at delta = 0 the pooled interval is the exactly-calibrated test. Only the injected-effect coverage column can see it. (b) MN vs Newcombe vs AC(z^2/4) on a balanced, non-sparse cohort differ by O(1/(npq)) ~ 1e-4 relative; distinguishing them needs M ~ 1e8. (c) Interval WIDTH is invisible to any FPR or power column -- two methods with identical decisions but 20% different widths score identically, and width is what a human reads. (d) COHERENCE is invisible unless the disagreement column of prediction 3 is added; the existing columns cannot express it. (e) Any defect that is a monotone function of the same statistic -- e.g. the N/(N-1) factor -- moves FPR by 1/(2N) and can never be measured.
open_questions: The MN N/(N-1) factor: keep it (matches the published method and the R/SAS implementations a golden test would use), drop it (Farrington-Manning; makes Z(0) bit-identical to the classical pooled z so no reported p-value moves at all), or apply it to both the interval and the p-value (coherent, but the printed p then differs from the classical one by a relative 1/(2N))? This is a decision, not a derivation; I lean to applying it to both or to neither, and to documenting which.

An always-valid / anytime-valid overlay that consumes a fixed (effect, SE) pair cannot consume a score interval: a score interval is asymmetric and has no single SE. Either the sequential transform must be re-derived on the score scale (a confidence sequence built from the score statistic), or the fixed-horizon and sequential intervals use different machinery and can disagree about the same data. [Contamination: I know such an overlay exists only from injected material; the incompatibility is derived.]

Multiplicity. Under Bonferroni the per-comparison alpha is fixed in advance, so 'the interval at alpha/m excludes zero' is a coherent statement. Under BH the threshold is data-dependent, so there is no fixed alpha to build an interval at, and 'the interval excludes zero' is not an interval statement at all -- it is a p-value statement wearing an interval's clothes. If the engine mixes the two, that is a larger coherence problem than pooled-vs-unpooled and it is not solved by any choice in this document. [Contamination: BH specifically came from injected material.]

Is the unit really one Bernoulli draw? If conversion is counted per session while randomization is per user, or if a unit can convert more than once, the metric is overdispersed and every SE here understates the truth -- by a factor that no choice of pooled/unpooled/score affects. The A/A permutation WILL see this (it permutes units, so it inherits the true within-unit correlation), which means an A/A calibration that comes out liberal should first be read as evidence about the unit definition, not about the interval method.

Root-find robustness: is Z(d)^2 - z^2 guaranteed to have exactly two sign changes on the feasible range? For degenerate cells (x_j at 0 or n_j) the constrained MLE sits on a boundary and the function's shape changes. A bracketing scan plus a documented fallback is needed, and the fallback's behaviour should itself be a test.

Planner consistency: if the analysis rule becomes score-based, the power/MDE machinery (which is Wald-based) no longer inverts the rule that will be applied, so a stated MDE will not be the effect the analysis actually detects at the stated power. The discrepancy is O(z^2/N) balanced and larger under imbalance -- probably ignorable, but it should be measured rather than assumed.

Should the relative interval be reported at all when x1 is very small? The width law z*sqrt(1/x1 + 1/x2) says a relative effect is unidentified below a few hundred conversions per arm; a displayed [-72%, +260%] is technically correct and practically misleading. A suppression threshold stated in CONVERSIONS (not units) may be better UX than a wider interval.

Odds ratio: the same constrained-MLE score construction generates it, and for small p it is numerically close to RR. Whether the engine should offer it, and whether offering three coherent scales is clarity or clutter, is a product question this derivation does not settle.

Annals of Statistics 30:160-201. https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-30/issue-1/Confidence-Intervals-for-a-binomial-proportion-and-asymptotic-expansions/10.1214/aos/1015362189.full -- the formal two-term Edgeworth expansions separating the smooth and oscillatory components of coverage error.

Approximate interval estimation of the ratio of binomial parameters.
